item.title: Why Conversations Leave Us Emotionally Exhausted
item.description:
Emotional Validation

Why Conversations Leave Us Emotionally Exhausted

Being present means staying out of someone else’s story.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional exhaustion often comes from inserting ourselves into others' stories during conversations.
  • Our brains naturally make associations, but acting on them too soon can shift focus from listening.
  • Genuine support means staying present with someone's story, not immediately relating or solving.
  • The urge to help can sometimes be about soothing our own discomfort, not just aiding others.
Source: Sound On/Pexels

When we think about being present, we usually picture putting our phones away, slowing down, or practicing mindfulness. We imagine learning to quiet our thoughts and focus on the moment. But there’s another kind of presence that rarely gets discussed. It’s the kind that happens in our conversations. And it may be one of the overlooked reasons so many helpers, parents, leaders, and partners end conversations feeling emotionally drained.

Our Brains Naturally Form Associations During Conversations

Picture this: Someone begins sharing something difficult. Before they’ve even finished their sentence, your brain has already gotten to work.

"That happened to me once."

"I know exactly what they should do."

"I should tell them what worked for me."

"This reminds me of..."

This isn’t because we’re selfish or poor listeners. It’s because our brains are designed to make connections. New information naturally connects to past experiences, helping us make sense of the world through memory and meaning.

From a neuroscience perspective, this process is exactly how our brains help us understand and navigate the world. Research on memory and cognition shows that our experiences are not stored as isolated pieces of information. Instead, memories are organized through interconnected networks, meaning that encountering something new can automatically activate related memories, emotions, and past experiences. This process, often referred to as associative memory, allows us to quickly interpret information and find meaning in what we are experiencing.

Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

When someone shares something difficult with us, our brain naturally searches for connections. It may retrieve a similar situation we experienced, a lesson we learned, or a solution that helped us in the past.

These associations are not a problem. In many ways, they are part of what allows us to relate to and empathize with others. The challenge is that we often mistake the first association our brain offers for the response the other person needs from us. Too often, we begin speaking from the association instead of continuing to listen from the present moment.

Without realizing it, the conversation shifts. We move from curiosity to commentary or from witnessing someone’s experience to comparing it with our own. We don’t simply notice these associations. We engage with them. We treat them as something that needs to be acted on, and before we realize it, we’ve projected our internal experience into the conversation. We haven’t left the conversation physically, but mentally we’ve stepped into our own story. That subtle shift changes everything.

The Difference Between Relating and Listening

As a therapist, I often see people mistake relating for listening. We assume that sharing our own experience communicates empathy. Sometimes it does, but timing is everything. When we relate too quickly, we unintentionally redirect the conversation before the other person has fully shared what they’re carrying.

Validation creates space. It doesn’t require us to silence our own thoughts. It asks us to acknowledge them, press pause, and stay present with the message and emotion the other person is sharing. This is the crossroads between supporting and solving. It’s the difference between saying, “Tell me more about what that’s been like for you,” and, “I know exactly how you feel. When that happened to me…”

The intention may be the same, but the impact is very different. One of the core ideas in my Support, Don’t Solve framework is that support doesn’t require becoming part of someone else’s story. It requires staying with their story long enough for them to better understand it themselves. By creating space instead of filling it, we give people the opportunity to process, reflect, and discover what they truly need. That can be surprisingly uncomfortable. Sometimes our urge to help isn’t only about the other person. It’s also about us.

Watching someone struggle can bring up our own discomfort. We want to make things better. We want to feel useful. We want reassurance that we’re being a good parent, leader, partner, or friend. Offering advice gives us something to do. Sharing our own experience can make us feel connected, but it can also reassure us that we’re useful, competent, and needed. But occasionally, what looks like compassion is actually an attempt to regulate our own discomfort.

This is what I call control disguised as compassion.

Source: Karola G/Pexels

We interrupt with solutions before fully understanding the problem. We reassure before we’ve validated because reassurance relieves our discomfort faster than validation relieves theirs. We move people toward our timeline instead of allowing them to move through their own. Helping becomes something we do to relieve our discomfort rather than something we offer for theirs.

The irony is that genuine presence often feels less productive in the moment. It asks us to tolerate uncertainty and resist the urge to fill the silence. It asks us to trust that understanding is often more valuable than immediate advice. Active listening doesn’t mean you won’t have thoughts, memories, or ideas. It means you notice them without allowing them to take over the conversation.

How to Practice Genuine Presence in Conversations

There are always two conversations happening. One is happening in front of you. The other is happening inside your own mind. Presence is recognizing the second conversation without allowing it to replace the first. When we do this, something important happens. The other person feels heard rather than managed. They feel understood rather than redirected. And perhaps just as importantly, we stop taking ownership of experiences that were never ours to carry. Many of us leave difficult conversations emotionally exhausted because we quietly inserted ourselves into them. We replay what we should have said, wonder whether we gave the right advice, or feel responsible for outcomes that were never ours to control.

Presence keeps emotional ownership with its rightful owner.

We can care deeply without carrying someone else’s burden.

This takes practice, but you’ll have plenty of opportunities to practice. The next time someone shares something vulnerable, notice what happens inside your own mind. You’ll probably have a memory, an opinion, advice, or a story. Let those thoughts come. They’re doing exactly what brains do. Then let them wait. Stay with the other person just a little longer. Presence isn’t measured by how quickly you respond. It’s measured by how long you’re willing to stay in someone else’s world before inviting them into yours.

item.title: Freedom From Things
item.description:
Meditation

Freedom From Things

Finding liberation in the ever-changing nature of experience.

Posted July 25, 2026

Imagine a stick of incense burning. As you watch the rising smoke drift toward the sky, it may seem for a moment as if the smoke looks like something. But the smoke never actually assumes any fixed form. It is continuously moving, reshaping itself the very instant it seems to take on a particular shape. Our experience is just like this.

It’s strange because it seems as if there’s something here that’s being encountered, something we seem able to identify. From one perspective, we’re experiencing fixed, identifiable forms, both the supposed objects of the world that we think of as being more or less unmoving and the internal world of subjectivity. But when we feel the flow of experiencing, we can notice that what we’re labeling as and believing to be identifiable things are, like the rising incense, continuously dissolving and in that sense, utterly without form.

The world of experience and circumstance appears as something we can grasp hold of and render with words and concepts. But when we look a little more closely, we can see that this is only half of the story, for all the things we think of as having fixed, identifiable forms do not.

Forms seem to be present and recognizable. Things seem to be a certain way. But when we try to pin down what that way is, it moves away from us, shape-shifting like the rising smoke. Try it right now. Try to keep what you’re calling the present moment from becoming something else. Try to hold it in place long enough to identify and describe it, and you’ll see the absolute impossibility of that.

Thinking we know what things are turns out to be pure fantasy because what we think of as things are actually not things.

It’s strange because we seem to encounter experiences and circumstances that are holding still, at least long enough to partake of them. I mean, you go out to dinner with friends, have a rich conversation, pay the bill, drive home, go to sleep, wake up the next morning. Our lives seem to consist of actual things that we can know and describe. The world shows up with a kind of coherence. Things seem to be holding still, at least long enough to encounter them as things. And yet, they are not. The moment never actually coheres. It never becomes something that can be identified because it is never actually here. What we call the “present moment” cannot be found as some “thing” because of its inherent dynamism. Like the rising smoke of the incense, it never assumes any fixed shape or form owing to its constant movement.

Take what’s happening right now. You might describe the event as “sitting in whatever room or place you are in, reading these words.” OK, so here you are, reading in your room (or at the beach or in a coffee shop or wherever). That’s what you’re experiencing, right? But where are the last five seconds you described as sitting here reading? They’ve vanished, right? What about the last second? It’s gone too. And the last quarter of a second? One one-millionth of a second? Gone.

So ask yourself—exactly how long have you been where you imagine you are, doing whatever you imagine you are doing? There’s absolutely no way to grasp hold of this supposed moment and say anything definitive about it. Why? Because it isn’t here long enough to say a single thing about how or what it is.

It’s interesting, though, because as true as it is that what’s appearing cannot be found as some fixed form or pattern or shape, reality sure does look and feel like something coherent and stable. There seems to be a coherence to reality. We experience this undeniable sense that there are things that actually look like something. After all, we have a whole dictionary filled with words we use to place all this seeming coherence into the descriptive categories that we do.

It appears we can say something about what’s going on. I mean, I can tell you about my day, and you can tell me about yours, right? There’s a beauty and richness to this capacity we have to seemingly know what things are and use language to describe them to ourselves and others.

Yet, beautiful and enjoyable as it can be, we can’t really pull it off. Consider again the burning incense. Can you describe how the smoke looks—its shape, its position, its size, its texture? Or has the way the smoke seems to have shaped itself dissolved in the very instant it seemed to appear?

If I take the phrase, “I am sitting here in my chair, writing these words,” every word in that sentence rests upon the belief that it’s actually possible to resolve what each of those elements—me, the chair, sitting, writing—are. While it may seem as if resolving what things are is possible, when I look at my experience of whatever seems to be present, I am always met with the fact that reality never becomes anything in particular. What we call the arising of the moment is also its vanishing, and, in that sense, there is no definable moment that’s ever here.

This discovery that reality is here for no time is ultimately liberating. Why? Because our sense of being overwhelmed by or at the mercy of different things rests upon the belief that we can actually know there even is a thing in the first place to be at the mercy of or overwhelmed by, and there literally is not.

While life can no doubt show up as all the seemingly resolvable things it shows up as—things which can in turn be perceived as difficult, lacking, problematic, and so on, like the rising smoke from the incense—what we think of as the problematic aspects of life never actually become any of the things we imagine they’ve become. And therein lies our freedom—the freedom from things.

Adapted from my latest book, Everything Is the Doorway.

item.title: LSD Today for a Better Brain Tomorrow
item.description:
Psychedelics

LSD Today for a Better Brain Tomorrow

Lasting changes in brain function occur quickly after a single LSD treatment.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • Little is known about how brain function evolves in the days following a single administration of LSD.
  • A study in humans characterized acute and longer-term effects on perceptual processing and motor learning.
  • LSD showed significant selective improvements in motor skill performance.

Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) has joined a growing list of potent serotonergic system psychedelics that have emerged as promising treatments for some psychiatric disorders, including major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, and substance use disorders. Like other psychedelics, a single administration can produce therapeutic benefits that can persist for months, suggesting that LSD may have induced lasting changes in brain function. Animal studies suggest that these benefits are driven by changes in dendritic growth, synaptic plasticity, and neurotrophin (brain hormone) expression. LSD is thought to open a critical learning period, characterized by increased aspects of neuroplasticity, in which learning is more efficient for at least a few days after dosing (for more about LSD’s actions in the brain, read Your Brain on Food, How Chemicals Control Your Thoughts and Feelings).

Evidence of these changes in human subjects remains relatively limited. Little is known about how brain function and behavior evolve in the days following a single drug administration. A recent study investigated the lasting effects of LSD on motor learning and perceptual processing. Motor learning was assessed using a sequence typing task capturing both online learning during active practice and offline consolidation following practice. Perceptual processing was determined by examining the neurophysiological effects using auditory tetanization with electroencephalography and paired associative stimulation with transcranial magnetic stimulation. In addition, self-report measures included questionnaires on perceived stress and cognitive flexibility. Together, these approaches allowed the authors to characterize acute and longer-term effects on perceptual processing, motor learning, and psychological functioning for up to one week after a single dose of LSD in healthy subjects. Blood levels of the neurotrophin BDNF were determined to assess possible longer-term effects of LSD on this hormone that is known to be critical for the maintenance of neuroplasticity.

This highly rigourous study used a randomized, double-blind crossover design. Forty-five healthy participants between the ages of 21 and 55 received one dose of 100µg LSD and one inactive placebo.

This is the first study using healthy human subjects to demonstrate improvements in motor learning after a psychedelic drug. Overall, LSD induced mostly positive acute and lasting subjective effects, as well as transient side effects. As predicted by similar studies using psilocybin, LSD induced changes in neural activity that are associated with the disruption of early sensory processing and attentional allocation. Essentially, this is what is expected when the subjects are creating internally generated sensory signals, i.e., they’re hallucinating (Kometer et al., 2011). Acutely, LSD impaired the ability of the subjects to pay attention to salient or novel sensory inputs. LSD treatment also commonly causes muscle tension and shaking during its peak drug effects; the mechanisms underlying this effect are well known. Finally, there was no effect of LSD on BDNF levels. The lasting changes in brain function must depend upon changes in other neurotrophins.

The day after dosing, the subjects who received LSD showed significant selective improvements in motor memory consolidation. This change was specific to improvements in speed. There was no change in accuracy, suggesting that the effect on speed does not simply reflect a speed-accuracy trade-off. The authors speculated that these improvements showed either enhanced neuroplasticity or possibly the post-drug exposure effects on motivation, attention, and/or arousal of the subjects.

Animals given LSD also show improved motor skills and improved performance across different learning paradigms, including classical and operant conditioning, fear extinction, and social reward learning. An earlier study using human subjects (Ornelas et al., 2022) reported improvements in visuospatial learning and memory consolidation the day after dosing only 50µg of LSD. These findings mirror those discovered using animal studies and suggest that a single treatment with LSD may broadly enhance synaptic plasticity in brain regions critical for learning and paying attention. How long these benefits last remains to be determined.
